hook.line: Tomás has a letter from Altamira's lawyers and no idea how to answer it, so he takes it to don Hernando's table. He isn't there to help; he's there to be helped. In Spanish, that difference is one word.
hook.es: Don Hernando, vine para que me ayude con una carta.
hook.en: Don Hernando, I came so that you could help me with a letter. (formal)

examples.en: I came so that you could help me. (to a friend)

examples.es: Estudio español para hablar con mi abuela.
examples.en: I'm studying Spanish to talk with my grandmother.

examples.es: Hablo despacio para que mi papá me entienda.
examples.en: I speak slowly so that my dad understands me.

examples.es: Llamo a Hernando para preguntarle por el barrio.
examples.en: I'm calling Hernando to ask him about the neighbourhood.

examples.es: Llamo a Hernando para que me cuente del barrio.
examples.en: I'm calling Hernando so he'll tell me about the neighbourhood.

examples.es: Me levanto temprano para abrir el café.
examples.en: I get up early to open the café.

examples.es: Me levanto temprano para que Vale encuentre todo listo.
examples.en: I get up early so that Vale finds everything ready.

rule:
Before you write *para*, ask: who does the second thing?

The same person: *para* plus the plain verb.
*Vine para ayudar.* I came, I help.
*Llamo a Hernando para preguntarle.* I call, I ask.

Someone else: *para que* plus the wish form.
*Vine para que me ayudes.* I came, you help.
*Llamo a Hernando para que me cuente.* I call, he tells.

Watch the second pair. Hernando is in both sentences, but in the first one you do the asking. Mentioning a person doesn't change anything; only who acts does.

English blurs it: to help, for you to help, so you can help. Spanish always makes you pick one of two shapes.
smallPrint: Teachers call this the same subject or different subject rule: *para* plus infinitive versus *para que* plus subjunctive.

readAndPick.es: Traigo la torta para que la prueben.
options: I'm bringing the cake so you all can try it.
I'm bringing the cake to try it with you all.

readAndPick.es: Traigo la torta para probarla con ustedes.
options: I'm bringing the cake so you all can try it.
I'm bringing the cake to try it with you all.

readAndPick.es: Llamo a Hernando para que me cuente del barrio.
options: I'm calling Hernando to tell him about the neighbourhood.
I'm calling Hernando so he'll tell me about the neighbourhood.

readAndPick.es: Llamo a Hernando para preguntarle por el barrio.
options: I'm calling Hernando to ask him about the neighbourhood.
I'm calling Hernando so he'll ask about the neighbourhood.

readAndPick.es: Te mando la foto para que la veas.
options: I'm sending you the photo so I can see it.
I'm sending you the photo so you can see it. (to a friend)
You're sending me the photo so I can see it.

readAndPick.es: Me levanto temprano para abrir el café.
options: I get up early so Vale can open the café.
I get up early so they can open the café.
I get up early to open the café.

readAndPick.es: Mariana escribe para que la gente sepa la verdad.
options: Mariana writes to find out the truth.
Mariana writes so that people know the truth.

readAndPick.es: Escribo para entender lo que pasa.
options: I write to understand what's happening.
I write so you understand what's happening.

readAndPick.es: Le dejo las llaves a Vale para que cierre.
options: I'm leaving the keys with Vale so I can lock up.
I'm leaving the keys with Vale so she can lock up.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *ayudar* or *que me ayudes* and type the whole sentence: *Vine para ___.* (I came to help.)
yourTurn.why: You came and you help: one person, plain verb.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *verla* or *que la veas* and type the whole sentence, to a friend: *Te mando la foto para ___.* (so you can see it)
yourTurn.answer: Te mando la foto para que la veas.
yourTurn.why: Your friend does the seeing, so *para que la veas*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I'm studying Spanish to talk with my grandmother.
yourTurn.answer: Estudio español para hablar con mi abuela.
yourTurn.why: You study and you talk, so no *que*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I speak slowly so that my dad understands me.
yourTurn.answer: Hablo despacio para que mi papá me entienda.
yourTurn.why: Your dad does the understanding, so *para que* and *entienda*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: I'm leaving the keys with Vale so she can lock up.
yourTurn.answer: Le dejo las llaves a Vale para que cierre.
yourTurn.why: Vale locks up, so *para que cierre*. No *pueda* needed.

yourTurn.prompt: Change who does it. Now it's so that Vale finds everything ready: *Me levanto temprano para abrir el café.*
yourTurn.answer: Me levanto temprano para que Vale encuentre todo listo.
yourTurn.why: Vale is the one finding, so *para que* and the wish form *encuentre*.

yourTurn.prompt: Change who does it. Now you want to try the cake with them yourself: *Traigo la torta para que la prueben.* (to try it with you all)
yourTurn.answer: Traigo la torta para probarla con ustedes.
yourTurn.why: Back to one person, so drop *que* and use *probarla*.

pitfalls.wrong: Estudio español para que hablo con mi abuela.
pitfalls.right: Estudio español para hablar con mi abuela.
pitfalls.why: Almost. You study and you talk, so just *para hablar*.

pitfalls.wrong: Hablo despacio para mi papá entender.
pitfalls.right: Hablo despacio para que mi papá me entienda.
pitfalls.why: When someone else acts, Spanish needs *para que* and the wish form.

pitfalls.wrong: Le dejo las llaves a Vale para que cierra.
pitfalls.right: Le dejo las llaves a Vale para que cierre.
pitfalls.why: *Para que* takes the wish form: *cierre*, not *cierra*.

personal: Write two true lines that start the same way: one with *para* plus a verb (why you do something for yourself), one with *para que* (why you do it for someone else). Try *Estudio español para...* and *Estudio español para que...*
